english: The Rayleys, Lily Briscoe thought, as she squeezed out her tube of green. She gathered together what she knew of them. She saw their lives as a string of scenes. One took place on the staircase at dawn. Paul had come home early and gone to bed; Minta was out late. And there she was on the stairs at around three in the morning, wreathed, made up, garish. Paul came out in pajamas with a poker, in case it was burglars. Minta stood halfway up by a window eating a sandwich in the deathly early light, and there was a hole in the carpet. But what did they say to each other? Lily wondered, as if looking hard enough would let her hear. Something violent. While he talked, Minta kept on eating her sandwich, which was maddening. His words were indignant and jealous; he abused her in a mutter so the children wouldn’t wake—the two little boys. He looked withered and drawn; she looked flamboyant and careless. After the first year or so, things had come loose; the marriage had turned out rather badly.
danish_before_fix: Rayleyerne, tænkte Lily Briscoe, mens hun klemte sin tube grøn ud. Hun samlede, hvad hun vidste om dem. Hun så deres liv som en snor af scener. En af dem fandt sted på trappen ved daggry. Paul var kommet tidligt hjem og gået i seng; Minta var ude sent. Og dér stod hun på trappen ved tre-tiden om morgenen, med blomsterkrans, sminket, prangende. Paul kom ud i pyjamas med en ildrager, for det kunne være indbrudstyve. Minta stod halvvejs oppe ved et vindue og spiste en sandwich i det dødblege tidlige lys, og der var et hul i tæppet. Men hvad sagde de til hinanden? undrede Lily sig, som om det at se længe nok ville lade hende høre det. Noget voldsomt. Mens han talte, blev Minta ved med at spise sin sandwich, hvilket var til at blive gal af. Hans ord var forargede og jaloux; han skældte hende ud i en mumlen, så børnene ikke skulle vågne — de to små drenge. Han så udtæret og forpint ud; hun så bluskende og skødesløs ud. Efter det første års tid var tingene gået løs i fugerne; ægteskabet var gået ret dårligt.

english: Hares bored Minta, Lily thought. But Minta never gave herself away. She would never say a thing like that about chess in coffeehouses; she was much too self-aware, much too careful. Still, to go on with their story—by now the dangerous stage was behind them. Lily had stayed with them for a while last summer, and the car broke down, and Minta had to pass him his tools. He sat in the road fixing it, and the way she passed him the tools—businesslike, direct, friendly—was proof that all was well now. They were not “in love” anymore. No: he had taken up with another woman, a serious woman who wore her hair in a braid and carried a briefcase (Minta described her with gratitude, almost with admiration). She went to meetings and shared Paul’s views, which had grown more and more pronounced, on taxing land values and on a capital levy. That alliance, far from wrecking the marriage, had put it right. Clearly they were excellent friends, he sitting in the road and she handing him his tools.
danish_before_fix: Harer kedede Minta, tænkte Lily. Men Minta røbede aldrig sig selv. Hun ville aldrig sige sådan noget som det om skak på kaffehuse; hun var meget for selvbevidst, meget for forsigtig. Men for at fortsætte deres historie — nu var det farlige stadie overstået. Lily havde boet hos dem et stykke tid sidste sommer, og bilen var gået i stykker, og Minta havde måttet række ham hans værktøj. Han sad på vejen og reparerede den, og den måde, hun rakte ham værktøjet på — forretningsmæssigt, ligefremt, venskabeligt — var et bevis på, at alt var godt nu. De var ikke »forelskede« mere. Nej: han havde slået sig sammen med en anden kvinde, en alvorlig kvinde, der bar sit hår i en fletning og gik med en dokumenttaske (Minta beskrev hende med taknemlighed, næsten med beundring). Hun gik til møder og delte Pauls synspunkter, som var blevet mere og mere markante, om beskatning af jordværdier og om en kapitalafgift. Den alliance havde langt fra at ødelægge ægteskabet bragt det på ret køl. Det var tydeligt, at de var fortrinlige venner, han siddende på vejen og hun rækkende ham sit værktøj.

english: Still, she thought, it had been a narrow escape. She had been looking at the tablecloth when it came to her in a flash that she would move the tree to the middle, and that she need never marry anyone, and she had felt tremendous exultation. She had felt she could stand up to Mrs. Ramsay now—which shows what astonishing power Mrs. Ramsay had over you. She said, Do this, and you did it. Even her shadow in the window with James carried authority. Lily remembered how it had shocked William Bankes that she disregarded the significance of mother and son. Didn’t she admire their beauty? he asked. But William had listened, she remembered, with his wise child’s eyes, as she explained that she meant no irreverence: a light here called for a shadow there, and so on. She had no wish to belittle a subject that Raphael, they both agreed, had painted divinely. She wasn’t cynical. Far from it. Because he had a scientific mind, he understood—proof of an impartial intelligence that had pleased and comforted her enormously. So it was possible, then, to talk seriously to a man about painting. In fact, his friendship had been one of the pleasures of her life. She loved William Bankes.

Hun havde set på dugen, da det i et glimt faldt hende ind, at hun ville flytte træet ind i midten, og at hun aldrig behøvede at gifte sig med nogen, og hun havde følt en enorm jubel. Hun havde følt, at hun nu kunne stå fast over for fru Ramsay — hvilket viser, hvilken forbløffende magt fru Ramsay havde over én. Hun sagde: Gør dette, og man gjorde det. Selv hendes skygge i vinduet med James udøvede autoritet. Lily huskede, hvordan det havde chokeret William Bankes, at hun ignorerede betydningen af mor og søn. Beundrede hun ikke deres skønhed? spurgte han. Men William havde lyttet, huskede hun, med sine kloge barneøjne, mens hun forklarede, at hun ikke mente det respektløst: et lys her krævede en skygge dér, og så videre. Hun havde ingen lyst til at ringeagte et motiv, som Rafael, var de begge enige om, havde malet guddommeligt. Hun var ikke kynisk. Langt fra. Fordi han havde et videnskabeligt sind, forstod han det — et bevis på en upartisk intelligens, som havde glædet og trøstet hende umådeligt. Så det var altså muligt at tale alvorligt med en mand om maleri. Faktisk havde hans venskab været en af glæderne i hendes liv. Hun elskede William Bankes.

english: Lily looked at the drawing-room step now. Through William’s eyes she saw the shape of a woman, quiet and peaceful, her eyes cast down. She sat lost in thought, pondering (she was wearing gray that day, Lily thought). Her gaze was lowered. She would never raise it. Yes, thought Lily, looking hard, I must have seen her look that way—but not in gray, and not so still, or so young, or so peaceful. The figure came easily enough. She was astonishingly beautiful, William said. But beauty wasn’t everything. Beauty had this price: it came too easily and too completely. It stopped life still—froze it. You forgot the small agitations: the flush, the paleness, some strange twist, some light or shadow that made the face unrecognizable for an instant and yet added something you saw in it ever after. It was simpler to smooth all that away beneath beauty. But what did she look like, Lily wondered, when she clapped her deerstalker hat on her head, or ran across the grass, or scolded Kennedy, the gardener? Who could tell her that? Who could help her?

Hun sad fortabt i tanker og grublede (hun havde gråt på den dag, tænkte Lily). Hendes blik var sænket. Hun ville aldrig løfte det. Ja, tænkte Lily og så skarpt til, sådan må jeg have set hende se ud — men ikke i gråt, og ikke så stille eller så ung eller så fredfyldt. Skikkelsen kom let nok. Hun var forbløffende smuk, sagde William. Men skønhed var ikke alt. Skønhed havde den pris: den kom for let og for fuldstændigt. Den standsede livet — frøs det. Man glemte de små uroligheder: rødmen, bleghed, et eller andet sært spil, et eller andet lys eller en skygge, der gjorde ansigtet ukendeligt et øjeblik og dog føjede noget til, man så i det for altid siden. Det var enklere at stryge alt det glat under skønheden. Men hvordan så hun ud, undrede Lily sig, når hun smækkede sin jægerhat på hovedet, eller løb hen over græsset, eller skændte på Kennedy, gartneren? Hvem kunne fortælle hende det? Hvem kunne hjælpe hende?

english: She wanted to walk straight over and say, “Mr. Carmichael!” He would look up kindly, as he always did, out of his vague, smoky green eyes. But you only woke people when you knew what you wanted to tell them. And what she wanted to say was not one thing but everything. Small words that chopped the thought up into pieces said nothing at all. “About life, about death; about Mrs. Ramsay”—no, she thought, you could say nothing to anybody. The urgency of the moment always missed. Words fluttered off to the side and struck inches below the target. Then you gave up, and the idea sank back down, and you turned into what most middle-aged people become: cautious, secretive, with lines between the eyes and a look of permanent anxiety. Because how could you put these feelings of the body into words? How could you express that emptiness there? (She was looking at the drawing-room steps. They looked extraordinarily empty.) It was the body that felt it, not the mind. The physical sensations that came with the bare look of those steps had all at once turned extremely unpleasant. Wanting and not having sent a hardness, a hollowness, a strain right through her body. And then wanting and not having—wanting and wanting—how it wrung the heart, over and over! Oh, Mrs. Ramsay! she cried out without a sound, to that essence sitting by the boat, that abstraction made out of her, that woman in gray—as if to scold her for having gone, and then, having gone, for coming back. Thinking of her had seemed so safe. Ghost, air, nothing, something you could toy with easily and safely at any hour of the day or night—that was what she had been. And then suddenly Mrs. Ramsay reached out her hand and wrung the heart like this. Suddenly the empty drawing-room steps, the frill of the chair inside, the puppy tumbling about on the terrace, the whole wave and whisper of the garden, turned into curves and arabesques flourishing around a center of total emptiness.
danish_before_fix: Hun ville gå lige hen og sige: »Hr. Carmichael!« Han ville se op med venlighed, som han altid gjorde, ud af sine vage, røgede grønne øjne. Men man vækkede kun folk, når man vidste, hvad man ville fortælle dem. Og det, hun ville sige, var ikke én ting, men alt. Små ord, der hakkede tanken i stykker, sagde slet intet. »Om livet, om døden; om fru Ramsay« — nej, tænkte hun, man kunne intet sige til nogen. Øjeblikkets hastende karakter ramte altid ved siden af. Ordene flagrede til siden og slog ned nogle tommer under målet. Så gav man op, og idéen sank tilbage, og man blev til det, de fleste mennesker i middelalderen bliver: forsigtige, hemmelighedsfulde, med rynker mellem øjnene og et udtryk af vedvarende uro. For hvordan kunne man sætte ord på disse kropslige følelser? Hvordan kunne man udtrykke den tomhed dér? (Hun så på stuetrappen. Den så usædvanligt tom ud.) Det var kroppen, der følte det, ikke sindet. De fysiske fornemmelser, der fulgte med synet af de nøgne trin, var med ét blevet yderst ubehagelige. At ville have og ikke få sendte en hårdhed, en hulhed, en spænding gennem hele hendes krop. Og så at ville have og ikke få — at ville og ville — hvor det vred hjertet, igen og igen! Åh, fru Ramsay! råbte hun lydløst til den essens, der sad ved båden, den abstraktion, der var lavet af hende, den kvinde i gråt — som for at skælde hende ud for at være gået og så, da hun var gået, for at komme tilbage. At tænke på hende havde forekommet så trygt. Genfærd, luft, intet, noget man let og trygt kunne lege med på ethvert tidspunkt af dag eller nat — det var, hvad hun havde været. Og så pludselig rakte fru Ramsay hånden ud og vred hjertet sådan her. Pludselig forvandledes den tomme stuetrappe, kanten på stolen derinde, hvalpen, der tumlede rundt på terrassen, hele havens bølgen og hvisken til kurver og arabesker, der slyngede sig omkring et centrum af fuldkommen tomhed.

english: She had an odd idea that he did hear, after all, the things she couldn’t say. He was an unreadable old man, with his yellow-stained beard and his poetry and his puzzles, sailing calmly through a world that met all his needs; it seemed to her that he had only to lower his hand where he lay on the lawn to fish up whatever he wanted. She looked at her picture. That, presumably, would have been his answer: how “you” and “I” and “she” pass and vanish; nothing lasts; everything changes; but not words, not paint. And yet it would be hung in the attics, she thought; it would be rolled up and tossed under a sofa. Even so, even of a picture like that, it was true. You could say of this scrawl—perhaps not of the actual picture, but of what it tried to do—that it “remained forever.” That was what she was going to say; or rather, since the words sounded too boastful even to her once spoken, she was going to hint it without words. But when she looked at the picture, she was surprised to find she couldn’t see it. A hot liquid filled her eyes (at first she didn’t think of tears); it left her lips firm, but it thickened the air and ran down her cheeks. In every other way she was in complete control of herself—oh yes! Was she crying for Mrs. Ramsay, then, without being aware of any unhappiness? She turned to old Mr. Carmichael again. What was it, then? What did it mean? Could things push their hands up and grab you? Could the blade cut, the fist clench? Was there no safety? No learning the world’s ways by heart? No guide, no refuge—was it all miracle, and leaping off the top of a tower into the air? Could it be that, even for older people, this was life?—startling, unexpected, unknown? For one moment she felt that if the two of them stood up, here and now on the lawn, and demanded an explanation—why was it so short, why so impossible to explain—and demanded it violently, the way two fully equipped human beings might speak who should have nothing hidden from them, then beauty would roll itself up; the space would fill; those empty flourishes would take shape; if they only shouted loudly enough, Mrs. Ramsay would come back. “Mrs. Ramsay!” she said out loud. “Mrs. Ramsay!” Tears were streaming down her face.
danish_before_fix: Hun havde en underlig forestilling om, at han trods alt hørte de ting, hun ikke kunne sige. Han var en ulæselig gammel mand med sit gulplettede skæg og sin poesi og sine gåder, sejlende roligt gennem en verden, der opfyldte alle hans behov; det forekom hende, at han kun behøvede at sænke hånden, hvor han lå på plænen, for at fiske op, hvad han ønskede. Hun så på sit billede. Det ville formodentlig have været hans svar: hvordan »du« og »jeg« og »hun« går forbi og forsvinder; intet varer; alt forandrer sig; men ikke ord, ikke maling. Og dog ville det blive hængt op på loftet, tænkte hun; det ville blive rullet sammen og smidt ind under en sofa. Alligevel, selv om et billede som det, var det sandt. Man kunne sige om dette kluderi — måske ikke om selve billedet, men om det, det forsøgte — at det »forblev for evigt«. Det var det, hun ville sige; eller rettere, eftersom ordene lød for pralende selv for hende, når de var sagt, ville hun antyde det uden ord. Men da hun så på billedet, blev hun overrasket over at opdage, at hun ikke kunne se det. En hed væske fyldte hendes øjne (først tænkte hun ikke på tårer); den lod hendes læber stå faste, men den tykkede luften og løb ned ad hendes kinder. På alle andre måder havde hun fuldstændig kontrol over sig selv — åh ja! Græd hun så for fru Ramsay uden at være sig nogen ulykkelighed bevidst? Hun vendte sig igen mod gamle hr. Carmichael. Hvad var det så? Hvad betød det? Kunne ting skyde deres hænder op og gribe fat i én? Kunne klingen skære, næven knytte sig? Fandtes der ingen tryghed? Ingen mulighed for at lære verdens veje udenad? Ingen vejleder, ingen tilflugt — var det hele et mirakel, og et spring fra toppen af et tårn ud i luften? Kunne det være, at selv for ældre mennesker var dette livet? — opsigtsvækkende, uventet, ukendt? I et øjeblik følte hun, at hvis de to rejste sig, her og nu på plænen, og krævede en forklaring — hvorfor var det så kort, hvorfor så umuligt at forklare — og krævede den voldsomt, som to fuldt udrustede mennesker ville tale, der ikke burde have noget skjult for sig, så ville skønheden rulle sig sammen; rummet ville fyldes; de tomme udsmykninger ville tage form; hvis de bare råbte højt nok, ville fru Ramsay komme tilbage. »Fru Ramsay!« sagde hun højt. »Fru Ramsay!« Tårerne strømmede ned ad hendes ansigt.

En hed væske fyldte hendes øjne (først tænkte hun ikke på tårer); den lod hendes læber stå faste, men den tykkede luften og løb ned ad hendes kinder. På alle andre måder havde hun fuldstændig kontrol over sig selv — åh ja! Græd hun så for fru Ramsay uden at være sig nogen ulykkelighed bevidst? Hun vendte sig igen mod gamle hr. Carmichael. english: And now, little by little, the pain of wanting, and the bitter anger (at being called back just when she believed she would never grieve for Mrs. Ramsay again—had she missed her among the coffee cups at breakfast? Not at all), grew less. What their anguish left behind, as a remedy, was a relief that soothed in itself, and also, more mysteriously, a sense that someone was there—Mrs. Ramsay, freed for a moment of the weight the world had laid on her, lingering lightly beside Lily and then (for this was Mrs. Ramsay in all her beauty) lifting to her forehead a wreath of white flowers and going off with it. Lily squeezed her tubes again and attacked the problem of the hedge. It was odd how clearly she could see Mrs. Ramsay stepping, quick as always, across fields that were soft and purplish in their folds, full of flowers—hyacinths or lilies—among which she vanished. It was a trick of the painter’s eye. For days after hearing of her death, Lily had seen her like this, raising the wreath to her forehead and going off unquestioningly across the fields with her companion, a shadow. The sight, and the phrase, had power to comfort. Wherever she was—painting here in the country, or in London—the vision would come, and her eyes would half close, searching for something to rest the vision on. She would look down the railway carriage, or the bus; take a line from someone’s shoulder or cheek; look at the windows across the way; at Piccadilly strung with lamps at evening. All of it had been part of the fields of death. But there was always something—a face, perhaps, or a voice, or a newsboy calling the evening papers, _Standard, News_—that pushed through, snubbed her, woke her, and demanded, and in the end received, an effort of attention, so that the vision had to be made again and again. Now once more, driven by some instinctive need for distance and for blue, she gazed down at the bay, turning the blue bars of the waves into little hills and the more purple patches into stony fields. And once again, as always, something that didn’t belong startled her. In the middle of the bay was a brown speck. It was a boat—she saw that after a second. But whose? Mr. Ramsay’s, she answered. Mr. Ramsay: the man who had marched past her, aloof, with his hand raised, leading a procession, in those beautiful boots of his, asking for sympathy she had refused to give. By now the boat was halfway across the bay.

english: Apart from a streak of wind here and there, the morning was so fine that sea and sky seemed woven from a single fabric, as though sails were fixed high in the sky, or clouds had fallen into the sea. Far out, a steamer had drawn a huge scroll of smoke across the air, and it hung there, curling and circling ornamentally, as though the air were a delicate gauze that held things gently in its mesh and only rocked them softly this way and that. And, as sometimes happens in very fine weather, the cliffs seemed aware of the ships and the ships aware of the cliffs, as if they were passing some secret signal of their own between them. For though it was sometimes so near the shore, this morning in the haze the Lighthouse seemed immensely far away.

english: This old symbol—taking a knife and striking his father to the heart—he had always kept. Only now that he was older, as he sat glaring at his father in helpless fury, it was not the man himself he wanted to kill, not that old man reading. It was the thing that came down on him—perhaps without his knowing: that fierce, sudden harpy with black wings, its claws and beak all hard and cold, which struck and struck at you (he could feel that beak on his bare legs, where it had struck him as a child) and then flew off; and there he was again, an old man, very sad, reading his book. That was what he would kill; that was what he would strike to the heart. Whatever he did with his life—(and he felt he might do anything, as he looked at the Lighthouse and the distant shore)—whether he went into business or a bank, or became a lawyer, or ran some enterprise, that was what he would fight, what he would hunt down and stamp out: tyranny, despotism, as he called it—forcing people to do what they didn’t want to do, taking away their right to speak. How could any of them say, But I won’t, when he said, Come to the Lighthouse. Do this. Fetch me that. The black wings spread; the hard beak tore. And then, a moment later, there he was, sitting reading; and he might look up—you never could tell—perfectly reasonably. He might chat with the Macalisters. He might be pressing a gold coin into the hand of some freezing old woman in the street, James thought; he might be cheering at some fishermen’s sports day; he might be flinging his arms about in excitement. Or he might sit at the head of the table without a word from one end of dinner to the other. Yes, James thought, while the boat slapped and lazed about in the hot sun: there was a wasteland of snow and rock, very lonely and stern; and there, he had begun to feel quite often lately, whenever his father said something that took the others by surprise, were only two sets of footprints—his and his father’s. Only they knew each other. Then what was this terror, this hatred? He turned back among the many leaves the past had folded inside him, peering into the heart of that forest where light and shadow so dapple each other that every shape is warped, and you stumble along, now with the sun in your eyes, now in dark shade. He was searching for an image that would cool his feeling, set it apart, and round it off into something solid. Suppose, then, that when he was a child sitting helpless in his baby carriage, or on somebody’s lap, he had seen a cart crush someone’s foot, without meaning to, innocently? Suppose he had seen the foot first, smooth and whole in the grass; then the wheel; then that same foot, purple and crushed. But the wheel was innocent. And so now, when his father came striding down the hall early in the morning, banging on their doors to get them up to go to the Lighthouse, it came down over his foot, over Cam’s foot, over anyone’s foot. You just sat and watched.

Eller han kunne sidde for bordenden uden et ord fra den ene ende af middagen til den anden. Ja, tænkte James, mens båden klaskede og dovnede i den hede sol: der lå en ødemark af sne og klippe, meget ensom og streng; og der, det var han for nylig begyndt at føle ret ofte, hver gang hans far sagde noget, der overrumplede de andre, var kun to sæt fodspor — hans og hans fars. Kun de to kendte hinanden. Hvad var så denne rædsel, dette had? Han vendte tilbage mellem de mange blade, fortiden havde foldet inde i ham, og spejdede ind i hjertet af den skov, hvor lys og skygge plamager hinanden så, at enhver skikkelse bliver forvredet, og man snubler af sted, nu med solen i øjnene, nu i mørk skygge. Man sad bare og så på.

english: In the end he stopped thinking. He just sat there in the sun, his hand on the tiller, staring at the Lighthouse, unable to move, unable to brush off these grains of misery that kept settling on his mind one by one. It was as if a rope held him there, a rope his father had knotted, and the only way to escape was to take a knife and plunge it in. … But just then the sail swung slowly round and slowly filled; the boat seemed to shake herself, then to move off, half conscious, still in her sleep; and then she woke up and shot through the waves. The relief was enormous. They all seemed to move apart again and relax, and the fishing lines stretched tight at a slant over the side. But his father did not stir. He simply lifted his right hand high in the air, mysteriously, and let it drop back onto his knee, as if he were conducting some secret symphony.

english: So a great deal depends, then, Lily Briscoe thought as she looked at the sea—hardly a stain on it, so soft that the sails and clouds seemed set into its blue—a great deal depends, she thought, on distance: on whether people are close to us or far away. For her feeling about Mr. Ramsay altered as he sailed farther and farther across the bay. It seemed to be drawn out, stretched thin; he seemed to recede more and more. He and his children seemed to be swallowed by that blue, that distance. But here on the lawn, right beside her, Mr. Carmichael gave a sudden grunt. She laughed. He clawed his book up off the grass and settled himself back in his chair, puffing and blowing like a sea monster. That was quite another matter, because he was so close. And then all was quiet again. Surely they were up by now, she thought, glancing at the house; but nobody showed. Then again, she remembered, they had always vanished the moment a meal ended, off on their own affairs. It all went with this silence, this emptiness, the unreal feeling of early morning. Sometimes things were like that, she thought, pausing for a moment to look at the long glittering windows and the blue plume of smoke: they turned unreal. It was the same when you came back from a journey, or got over an illness—before habit had spun its web across the surface again, you felt that same startling unreality; felt something rise up. Life was never more vivid than then. You could be at your ease. You did not, thank goodness, have to march briskly across the lawn to greet old Mrs. Beckwith as she came out looking for a corner to sit in—“Oh good morning, Mrs. Beckwith! What a lovely day! Are you going to be so bold as to sit in the sun? Jasper’s hidden the chairs. Do let me find you one!”—and all the rest of the usual small talk. You did not have to talk at all. You glided, you shook out your sails (the bay was busy now, with boats setting out), between things and beyond them. It was not empty; it was full to the brim. She seemed to be standing in some substance up to her lips, to move in it, float in it, sink in it—yes, for these waters had no bottom. So many lives had spilled into them. The Ramsays’, the children’s, and all kinds of strays and scraps of things as well. english: Here on the grass, on the ground, she thought, sitting down and prodding a little colony of plantains with her brush, for the lawn was very rough. Here, sitting on the world, she thought. She could not rid herself of the sense that everything this morning was happening for the first time—perhaps for the last—just as a traveler on a train, even half asleep, knows as he gazes out of the window that he has to look now, because never again will he see that town, or that mule-cart, or that woman working in the fields. The lawn was the world; up here, on this high perch, the two of them were together, she thought, looking over at old Mr. Carmichael, who seemed to share her thoughts (though neither had said a word all this while). And perhaps she would never see him again. He was getting old. And he was getting famous too, she remembered, smiling at the slipper that hung from his foot. People said his poetry was “so beautiful.” They were bringing out things he had written forty years ago. There was a famous man now by the name of Carmichael, she thought with a smile—how many shapes one person could take on! In the newspapers he was that; here he was just as he had always been. He looked the same—a bit grayer, if anything. Yes, the same; and yet somebody had told her, she recalled, that when the news came of Andrew Ramsay’s death (a shell killed him in an instant; he would have been a great mathematician), Mr. Carmichael had “lost all interest in life.” What could that mean? she wondered. Had he gone marching through Trafalgar Square clutching a big stick? Had he sat alone in his room in St. John’s Wood turning page after page without reading a word? She had no idea what he had done when he heard that Andrew was dead, but she sensed it in him all the same. All they ever did was mumble to each other on the stairs, look up at the sky, and say it will be fine or it won’t be fine. Still, this was one way of knowing people, she thought: knowing the outline rather than the detail, the way you might sit in your garden and watch a hillside running purple down into the distant heather. That was how she knew him. She knew that something in him had changed. Not one line of his poetry had she ever read. Yet she felt she knew how it went: slow and sonorous, seasoned and mellow. It was about the desert and the camel, about the palm tree and the sunset. It was utterly impersonal; it had something to say about death and very little about love. He had a kind of aloofness. He asked very little of other people. Hadn’t he always lurched past the drawing-room window rather awkwardly, a newspaper under his arm, trying to dodge Mrs. Ramsay, whom for some reason he did not much like? Which was exactly why, of course, she always tried to make him stop. He would bow to her—pull up unwillingly and bow low. Irritated that he wanted nothing from her, Mrs. Ramsay would ask him (Lily could hear her) wouldn’t he like a coat, a rug, a newspaper? No, there was nothing he wanted. (Here he bowed.) english: He reached out his hand and lifted her from her chair. Somehow it seemed he had done this before—as though once, long ago, he had bent over in just the same way and lifted her out of a boat lying a few inches off some island, where the ladies had to be handed ashore like this by the gentlemen. It was an old-fashioned scene; it almost demanded crinolines and peg-top trousers. As she let him help her, Mrs. Ramsay had thought (so Lily supposed): the time has come. Yes, she would say it now. english: But it wore Mrs. Ramsay out and cowed her a little, the whizzing plates and the slamming doors. And sometimes long, rigid silences would come down between them. At such times she was in a mood that irritated Lily—half plaintive, half resentful; she seemed unable to rise calmly above the storm, or to laugh as the rest of them laughed; yet perhaps in her weariness she was hiding something. She brooded and said nothing. After a while he would start hovering stealthily wherever she was, prowling under the window where she sat writing letters or talking; for she made sure to be busy when he went by, and slipped away from him, and pretended she had not seen him. Then he would turn as smooth as silk, genial and charming, and try to win her over like that. She would still keep her distance, and now, for a little while, she would take on some of the pride and grand manners that her beauty gave her a right to and that she almost never showed; she would turn her head, glance over her shoulder like that, always with some Minta or Paul or William Bankes beside her. In the end he would stand outside the group, the very image of a starving wolfhound (Lily got up from the grass and stood looking at the steps and the window where she had seen him), and say her name—just once, exactly like a wolf barking in the snow. Still she held back. Then he would say it again, and this time something in his voice would stir her, and all at once she would leave them and go to him, and the two of them would walk off together among the pear trees and the cabbages and the raspberry beds. They would have it out between them. But in what postures, and with what words? Their relationship had such dignity that she and Paul and Minta turned away, hiding their curiosity and their unease, and set about picking flowers, throwing balls, chattering, until dinnertime—and there the two of them were, as usual, he at one end of the table and she at the other.

english: All at once the window she was watching went white with some light fabric behind it. So someone had come into the drawing room at last; someone was in the chair. That was interesting. It might be useful. Her mood was returning. You had to keep looking, without letting the intensity of feeling slacken for one second—the resolve not to be put off, not to be tricked. You had to grip the scene—like this—in a vise and let nothing get in to spoil it. What you wanted, she thought, dipping her brush with care, was to stay level with ordinary experience—to feel simply, that’s a chair, that’s a table—and yet, at the same moment, it’s a miracle, it’s an ecstasy. Perhaps the problem could be solved after all. Ah, but what had happened? A white ripple passed across the glass. The air must have stirred some frill of cloth in the room. english: Mr. Ramsay buttoned up his coat and rolled up his trouser legs. He took the big, clumsily wrapped brown paper parcel that Nancy had put together and sat holding it on his knee. Sitting like this, all ready to land, he gazed back at the island. With his long sight he could perhaps see quite plainly that shrunken leaf-shape standing on end on a plate of gold. What could he see? Cam wondered. To her it was only a blur. What was he thinking now? she wondered. What was he searching for, so fixedly, so intently, so silently? The two of them watched him as he sat there hatless with his parcel on his knee, staring and staring at the fragile blue shape, which looked like the vapor of something that had burned itself away. What do you want? both of them wanted to ask. Both of them wanted to say, Ask us for anything and we’ll give it to you. But he did not ask them for anything. He sat looking at the island, and he might have been thinking, We perished, each alone, or he might have been thinking, I have reached it. I have found it; but he said nothing.

english: “He has landed,” she said aloud. “It is finished.” Then old Mr. Carmichael heaved himself up, puffing a little, and stood beside her like some old pagan god, shaggy, weeds in his hair and the trident (it was only a French novel) in his hand. He stood next to her at the edge of the lawn, his great bulk swaying slightly, and, shading his eyes with his hand, said, “They will have landed,” and she felt she had been right. They had had no need to speak. They had been thinking the same things, and he had answered her without her asking him anything. There he stood, spreading his hands over all the frailty and suffering of mankind; she thought he was looking out, tolerantly, compassionately, over their final fate. Now he has crowned the occasion, she thought, as his hand slowly dropped—as though she had watched him let fall from his great height a wreath of violets and asphodels, which drifted slowly down and came to rest at last on the earth.
